subtitle: How routers learn the cheapest path: by knowing the whole map, or by asking their neighbours.

fwd.body:
A router really does two quite different jobs, and you will be tempted to mix them up. Forwarding is the per-packet act of looking up the destination in the forwarding table and choosing the output port: fast, done in hardware. Routing is the slower process that builds that table. Think of forwarding as following road signs and routing as drawing the map.

Routes can be static (configured by hand) or dynamic (learned by a routing protocol). Within an organisation routers use an interior protocol (RIP, OSPF, EIGRP); between organisations the Internet uses the exterior protocol BGP. So which is done for every packet? Forwarding.
keynotes: Forwarding is the per-packet lookup of the destination in the forwarding table, done in hardware; routing is the slower process that builds the table.
Routes can be static (configured by hand) or dynamic (learned by a routing protocol).
Interior protocols (RIP, OSPF, EIGRP) work within an organisation; the exterior protocol BGP works between organisations.

ls.body:
One way to find the cheapest route is to hold the whole map in your hand. That is link-state routing (OSPF): every router floods the state of its links, so all routers hold the same map, and then each runs Dijkstra’s algorithm to find least-cost paths from itself. The method is patient: repeatedly settle the nearest unsettled node and relax its neighbours.

On the textbook graph from node u the costs to v, x, w, y, z come out as 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, and the route to z is u→x→y→z. Watch the tree of shortest paths grow in the figure. Dijkstra’s algorithm requires that link costs be non-negative.
keynotes: In link-state routing (OSPF) every router floods the state of its links so all hold the same map, then runs Dijkstra’s algorithm.
Dijkstra repeatedly settles the nearest unsettled node and relaxes its neighbours; it requires non-negative link costs.
On the textbook graph from u the costs to v, x, w, y, z are 2, 1, 3, 2, 4 and the route to z is u→x→y→z.

dv.body:
The other way is to know only your neighbours and ask them. It is how rumours travel, and surprisingly it works. In distance-vector routing (RIP) each router knows only its own links and its neighbours’ tables. Periodically it recomputes D(i,j) = min over neighbours k of [cost(i,k) + D(k,j)]. Information spreads one hop per round, and the tables converge to the same answers as Dijkstra. In the figure, amber entries improved this round.

The weakness is slow bad news. When a link fails, routers can keep fooling each other and count upward forever: the count-to-infinity problem. It is mitigated by split horizon and a small maximum hop count (RIP: 15). Can you see why a limit of 15 hops helps? It declares “infinity” early.
keynotes: In distance-vector routing (RIP) each router knows only its links and its neighbours’ tables and recomputes D(i,j) = min over neighbours k of [cost(i,k) + D(k,j)].
Information spreads one hop per round and the tables converge to the same answers as Dijkstra.
Count-to-infinity after a link failure is mitigated by split horizon and a small maximum hop count (RIP: 15).

protocols.body:
Let’s meet the cast. RIP: distance vector, hop count, 15 max. OSPF: link state, areas, fast convergence. EIGRP: Cisco’s advanced distance vector. BGP: path-vector between autonomous systems; it is policy-driven, not cost-driven, because the Internet is a collection of competing companies.

Two helpers work behind the scenes. ARP maps IP to MAC on a link, resolving the next hop on each link as the figure shows. ICMP reports errors and powers ping and traceroute. What does ARP do? It asks “who has this IP address?” and learns the MAC address that answers.
keynotes: RIP is distance vector with hop count (15 max); OSPF is link state with areas and fast convergence; EIGRP is Cisco’s advanced distance vector.
BGP is path-vector between autonomous systems and is policy-driven, not cost-driven.
ARP maps IP to MAC on a link; ICMP reports errors and powers ping and traceroute.

cc.body:
What happens when you and everyone else drive onto the motorway at once? Queues build, and cars get turned away. When offered load exceeds capacity, network queues grow and packets are dropped. Control can be open-loop, with traffic shaping by a leaky bucket or token bucket, or closed-loop, using feedback such as TCP’s window (next lesson).

A token bucket lets bursts through up to its depth, then enforces the average rate. Say it adds tokens at 100 packets/s and holds at most 50. The source can send 50 packets at once, then 100 per second sustained. A leaky bucket, by contrast, smooths traffic by letting packets out at a steady rate.
keynotes: When offered load exceeds capacity, queues grow and packets are dropped.
Control can be open-loop (traffic shaping with a leaky or token bucket) or closed-loop (feedback such as TCP’s window).
A token bucket at 100 packets/s holding at most 50 allows a burst of 50 packets, then 100 per second sustained.

summary.body:
Three lines to remember, and you can discuss routing with confidence.

  • Forwarding = lookup; routing = table building.
  • Link state: full map + Dijkstra. Distance vector: neighbours’ tables + Bellman–Ford.
  • BGP glues autonomous systems together by policy.
keynotes: Forwarding is lookup and routing is table building.
Link state uses the full map with Dijkstra; distance vector uses neighbours’ tables with Bellman–Ford.
BGP glues autonomous systems together by policy.
